en: And will destroy my san of cattle.
Come, my senior wife, hear me:
Unless this son ceases his wildness,
He will dig my pit.
If this son of yours grows,
He will boil my misery,
He will show me wonders.
My stores gathered from livestock,
If this son of yours grows,
He will utterly ruin me!
This son's manner is such:
Dust rises from his walking,
Life departs at his voice.
When he shouts, no human ear can bear it.
The boys who trade blows with him,
He drives to crouch like hares on the ground.
Of the boys who fall into his hands,
Not one comes out alive.
Your child will bring calamity;
This ruin will reach everyone.
There is a fortress on the slope;
These Kalmyk people are numerous.
‘This Burut's child
Has turned out wild,’ will they not say?
In the end, will they not devour me?
Helping one another, living together,
My Kalmyks were a fine people.
Where I dug gold and grew rich,
My Altay was a fine land.
Since coming to this Altay,
My fortune has filled and grown strong.
All four kinds of livestock
Have grown into a san of cattle.
Your son will scatter my herds,
He will drain my strength.
‘Your son is wild,’ they will say;
The Kalmyks will seize me,
Have me dragged along the road,
They will split me among the Dangyts.
Taking a crescent-crested banner,
They will bring havoc to the village.
Leaving not one of our dwindling lives,
They will strike and finish us all.
If you live, you will see:
He will bring hardship upon our heads!”
The noble senior wife Chyyyrdy
Then rose and spoke:
“My hero,
Do not trouble your thoughts over the child.
You have come to find a burden,
My lord, the child granted at death's door!
This gray-pied goshawk, this darling,
Do not find a burden, hey, my lord,
This morning star granted at death's door.”
The noble senior wife Chyyyrdy,
After her lord had spoken thus,
From her quail-like black eyes
Tears fell one by one.
Before she could close her mouth,
Before she could stop her tears,
There was Oshpur, chief of the shepherds;
That Oshpur came.
The senior wife stood and saw him come.
He turned his thoughts elsewhere;
Rich Jakyp handed over to Oshpur
The child named Chong Jindi.
Chyyyrdy wept and cried aloud,
Hanging her belt about her neck,
Pleading, calling “Oshpur-bay!”:
“My dear rich Oshpur,
You were a giant lying in the valley,
In charge of rich Jakyp's many sheep.
We had much wealth, but no child.
This child granted at death's door,
There is no way to restrain his wildness.
I made a silk coat; put it on him.
Among the horses is Toruchaar;
Catch that racing steed and mount him on it.
Fasten the Kalmyks' stone upon his crown.
I entrust him to your hands;
Raise him another four years!”
After Oshpur took the child,
After rich Jakyp remained there,
Mounting him on Toruchaar,
Dressing him in the finest silk,
Trusting his fate, toward the sheep
Warrior Oshpur led him away.
When Manas went to Oshpur,
He had not yet become Manas;
Your warrior had not yet won the name Manas.
Going to Oshpur, your gray-maned hero
Grew to manhood and became a warrior,
Became the equal of other men's sons.
He turned out a darkly burning ember;
Among the Black Kalmyks and Manchus
There was no such wild one.
One day Manas flew into a rage,
Beat the shepherds,
Beat the horse herder.
The shepherd fled in alarm;
All the horse herders,
“The Burut Chong Jindi is coming!” they said,
And fled in gawky haste.
Insistently calling himself Manas,
He gathered sheep and devised a plan.
Forty boys from the shepherds,
That Manas gathered them,
Slaughtered sheep on the steppe,
And Manas would not stop feasting.
Bumping along on calves,
A throng of boys gathered.
Manas began the revelry.
“Call me ‘My lord!’” he said;
Those boys' calves,
He slaughtered every one.
From this he began his mischief.
To a boy who called him “Lord,”
His felt cloak, with a proud air,
He would give there on the steppe.
At that time, Manas's
Wish was granted by God.
At that time, your Manas
Had reached twelve years of age.
Wearing a coat no bullet could pierce,
Riding a horse such as Toruchaar from the herd,
At that time the lion Manas
Could find no mountain to hurl himself against,
Could find no enemy to fight,
Could find no head to tear off,
Could find no stone to bite,
Utterly excited and carried away,
Unable to restrain his wild frenzy,
The dear lion of surpassing fortune,
This was where he made his sport.
“Call me ‘My lord!’” he said,
Making himself known,
Making those who knew him laugh.
On the open steppe, forty foot-lengths,
He had the customary ordo circle drawn.
Showing his gray-maned fierceness,
Of the many sheep Oshpur tended,
He slaughtered a thousand lambs.
“Call me ‘Hero!’” he said;
Fattened lambs, their sweet heads,
He set them boiling furiously.
Playing ordo, shooting knucklebones,
These were the gray-maned hero's deeds.
In the mire of broad Altay,
His forty boys beside him,
When the sun sank shimmering,
When living creatures and beasts
Lay without stirring,
Your gray-maned hero among the boys,
Sleeping propped on his elbow,
Taking a little nap and rest,
Pillowing his head on a white saddle,
Turning his head toward the qibla,
Noble Manas, your gray-maned hero,
Fell into a giant's sleep.
Until the sun stood at midmorning,
The joyous one slept soundly.
Before Manas rose from sleep,
The giant horse herder Kanjar-kol,
That accursed fellow arrived.
The piebald stallion beneath him,
That stallion was terribly swift.
“If I give its mouth free rein,
It will fly like a bird,” he said.
Look at that mad wretch:
He had loaded himself with sand.
His head was like a traveling kettle,
His brows like dogs lying down.
His black cudgel, his mace,
He grasped and whirled it.
Rushing at the forty boys,
He charged and attacked.
When they saw the giant Kanjar's form,
The forty boys fled screaming,
Not merely flesh, they had no faces left;
All the boys fled in a scattering rush.
The fleeing boys ran about,
Pleading with Khan Manas.
Manas woke from sleep,
Turned upon his right side,
Lifted his head and looked,
Looked to the boys' safety.
All the boys had fled.
Having caught four of the boys,
Dismounting from his stallion, that giant
Had pinned the four boys down.
He had slaughtered the four in a row,
And all the meat laid by for food,
He skewered it and ate his fill.
Seeing this, mighty Manas,
Startled by that wrestler,
Saddled Toruchaar,
Put on his battle clothes.
“I shall play mounted wrestling,” he said;
The reckless boy rejoiced.
Wrath rising, his eyes flashing,
His thirst for blood truly seized him.
His gleaming teeth, like a door,
Teeth unlike those of other people,
Bared themselves brightly.
His black cudgel, his mace,
Your boy grasped and whirled it.
Girding his waist firmly,
Striking Toruchaar once on the flank,
Breaking the ground beneath his tread,
Galloping toward the wrestler,
He turned Toruchaar's head.
When he reached that wrestler,
He stood and spoke these words:
“Your father's grave, giant Kanjar!
You are a horse herder, I a shepherd.
Destroying all the boys,
Cease this violence!
You plundered and ate my meat.
Even if you were twelve wrestlers,
Now vultures will peck your face.
Hey, giant Kanjar, stop!
Unless you agree to stop,
I shall make a spectacle now!”
As Manas was speaking,
The giant Kanjar rose.
The accursed giant Kanjar,
Treading heavily, hunched forward;
Of the forty boys, four
Lay dead, sprawled out.
While the children lay dead,
Would your Manas stand and watch?
“Your father's grave, giant Kanjar!
We were forty-one boys on the steppe,
Boiling lamb on the steppe,
People simply playing.
To force your way and eat your fill of meat,
To lay four boys sprawling,
To kill them for no reason,
Your mares upon the hills,
Did we raid and scatter them?
Did we mount your stallion and flee?
Is havoc what you want?
You attacked us yourself, looming large.
Now you will see wonders from me!”
Shouting and roaring three times,
Raising the battle cry “Manas!”
The black mace big as a house,
He grasped and whirled it.
Charging in at Kanjar,
He struck him on the very crown.
When he took Manas's mace blow,
His head burst into fragments.
The wrestler fell to the ground,
His life departed with a shriek.
He slaughtered the wrestler and laid him low.
